opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and they all come back to the economics of getting things wrong.

First, the cost of a bug in hardware is enormous and largely irreversible. With software you can push a patch overnight. With a chip, once you tape out, a bug can mean a respin costing tens of millions of dollars and months of delay, or in the worst case a recall. People still cite the Pentium floating-point division bug from the nineties as the cautionary tale. So the industry already has a strong incentive to prove correctness, not just test for it.

Second, formal verification is already part of the culture in chip design, unlike most software engineering. Big semiconductor companies have formal verification teams, they use model checkers and theorem provers, and they write specifications and properties for things like floating-point units, cache coherence protocols, and arithmetic circuits. So the problem isn't convincing them that formal methods matter. The problem is that it's incredibly labor-intensive. Verification can consume more engineering effort than design itself, and the people who can write good formal specs and guide a prover through a hard proof are extremely scarce. That's exactly the bottleneck AI can relieve.

Third, the complexity keeps exploding. Chips today, especially AI accelerators, have more custom logic, more heterogeneous components, and much faster design cycles because everyone is racing. Simulation-based testing covers a vanishingly small fraction of the state space. You can run billions of test vectors and still miss the corner case. Formal methods give you exhaustive guarantees, but they don't scale with human effort alone.

And finally, hardware is a relatively well-structured domain for AI-driven reasoning. The semantics are precise, the specifications are often mathematical, and you have a checker that tells you unambiguously whether a proof is correct. That's the same reason we're excited about AI for mathematics: when you have a verifier, you can let the model explore, generate proofs, fail, and learn, and you never have to worry about trusting a hallucination, because the proof either checks or it doesn't.

So when you put it together, chips are where the pain is most acute, the willingness to pay is highest, the formal infrastructure already exists, and the talent shortage is most severe. That makes it a natural first place where AI-assisted formal verification can deliver real value, before it spreads to software and other safety-critical systems.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to the cost of being wrong. In software, if you ship a bug, you patch it. You push an update, users download it, life goes on. In chips, once you've taped out, the design is literally etched into silicon. If there's a bug in the logic, you're looking at a respin that costs tens of millions of dollars and months of delay, and that's if you're lucky and catch it before it reaches customers. Think about the Pentium FDIV bug, or more recently some of the security flaws in processors. Those are not patchable in the same way.

So the chip industry already knows it needs verification. It's not like we have to convince them. Formal verification has been used in hardware for decades, much more seriously than in software, precisely because the stakes forced the industry's hand. But the way it's done today is extremely labor-intensive. You have teams of verification engineers, often more verification engineers than design engineers on a project, writing properties, hand-tuning proofs, fighting with tools that time out on anything beyond a certain complexity. Verification is somewhere around 60 to 70 percent of the total development cost on a modern chip. That's an enormous amount of highly skilled human effort going into something that is, in principle, a mathematical task.

And the designs keep getting more complex. You have heterogeneous architectures, AI accelerators with novel dataflow, chiplets, security requirements layered on top. The verification burden is growing faster than the number of people who can do it. There's a real talent bottleneck. The people who are good at formal hardware verification are rare, and training them takes years.

So when you put those things together, you have a domain where the demand for mathematical guarantees is already high and well understood, the cost of failure is catastrophic and irreversible, and the current process is dominated by scarce human labor doing structured reasoning. That's almost the ideal shape for an AI system that can actually do formal mathematics. In software, you often have to argue people into caring about proofs at all. In chips, they're already paying the price. They just need the tools to be dramatically better.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest reason is the cost of getting something wrong. In software, you can often ship a patch. In chips, once you’ve taped out and manufactured the hardware, a bug can mean a very expensive redesign and months of delay. So there’s a strong incentive to catch errors before that point.

At the same time, chips are incredibly complex, and simulation can only explore so many possible behaviors. Formal verification gives you a way to prove that a design satisfies particular properties, but writing those properties and getting the proofs to work requires specialized expertise. That makes verification a bottleneck.

So the opportunity for AI is to help with that labor-intensive work—formulating properties, developing proofs, and interpreting failures—while a formal tool checks the result. You’re not relying on the AI being right; you’re using it to make a rigorous verification process more accessible and efficient. In chips, the cost of errors makes that especially valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it comes down to the cost of getting something wrong. In software, you can often ship an update. With a chip, once you’ve taped out and manufactured it, a bug can mean a very expensive redesign. So there’s a strong incentive to establish correctness before you get to that point.

At the same time, the designs are incredibly complex, and formal verification takes a lot of specialized effort. You have to write the right specifications, express the properties you care about, and help the tools handle the complexity. That creates an opportunity for AI to reduce the human work involved.

The key distinction is that the AI doesn’t have to be the authority on correctness. It can propose a property or a proof step, and a formal tool can check it. You still need to make sure the specification captures what you actually intended, but that combination is compelling in a domain where mistakes are so costly.
